first_editorial_passes.verdict_before: The page had useful primary passages and an eight-stop navigation, but its 4,511 visible words repeatedly explained the same moral. It presented Socrates through a cinematic martyr story, treated disputed history as settled, misclassified the Phaedo, reduced the cave to enlightened people being punished, and named translations inconsistently. Its h1 was only 'Plato', while the full title was different, and its approximately 25-minute reading claim overstated its actual length.
important_fixes: Rebuilt all eight stops around particular passages rather than a repeated examination/cost/cure moral. Replaced the movie-theater opening with the less familiar requirement that the ideal city's educated philosophers return to govern.

Separated Plato's literary Socrates from the historical person. Identified the Apology as Plato's version of the defense speech, placed Phaedo with the usual middle-period grouping, and qualified the chronology as a scholarly model.
Replaced the absolute claim that Socrates only asked questions with his actual admission of limited ignorance. Kept craftsmen's genuine expertise and his positive moral judgment at Apology 29b.

Removed exact jury counts, confidence that exile or a modest fine would have saved him, and the implication that the Prytaneum proposal was his only alternative. Explained the later guaranteed fine at 38b.

Restored all parts of the religious indictment and the divine sign. Political suspicion is relevant background, not proof that the accusation concealed a political prosecution; the accusers' speeches are unavailable.

Replaced the Crito's compressed slogan with a verified Jowett passage and separated the principle against retaliation from the disputed premise that escaping harms the Laws. Addressed the tension with disobedience in the Apology.

Presented the Phaedo's immortality discussion through Simmias and Cebes' objections. Removed the inference that serenity proves the argument and the claim that the last words contain eight Greek words.

Verified Grube's 'we owe' last words against a publisher chapter identifying Complete Works. Compared them with Jowett's 'I owe', while leaving the offering's meaning unresolved and naming Gregory Nagy's alternative reading.
Removed the claim that the cave explains the historical prosecution. Marked a possible allusion to Socrates' death as an interpretation. Shortened its opening extract to exact Jowett wording.
Explained Forms with Phaedo's equal sticks and stones, and included Plato's own Parmenides objections. Avoided presenting Forms as perfect physical copies of everything.

Added the distinction between philosophers educated by the ideal city and those who owe it no educational debt. Explained reluctant rule and its objection concerning the authority of a selected group.
Made title, og:title, and h1 identical; made both descriptions fit the actual four-dialogue reading; advertised eight stops and eleven minutes rather than implying that all excerpts use Grube.

Fixed the existing jump-navigation/scroll-spy mismatch in js/plato.js. The same 12px offset now governs scrolling and recognition, includes the shared rail's computed top inset, and rounds the destination upward. Added aria-expanded state and Escape focus restoration.

length_decision.rationale: Eight distinct textual encounters earned their place. Repeated summaries, several redundant translation panels, the theatrical opening, reconstructed votes, biographical color, and the martyr-story closing did not. The five-pass edit removed more than ten percent from the full rewrite without losing an argument.
length_decision.advertised_read_time: 11 min, allowing roughly 225 visible words per minute and slower reading of the short passages

voice_changes: Monotone pass: replaced slogans about diagnosis/cure, composure as a conclusion, and a clever teacher-versus-darkness ending with primary details and stated limits.

Opening deletion pass: retained the opening because it contains the specific, less familiar civic obligation at 519c to 520e; deleted its summarizing final sentence and compressed the general overview.
Generic-sentence pass: removed exhortations to examine everything, modern screen metaphors, casual caricatures of Xenophon and Aristophanes, and repetitive moral takeaways.
Ten-percent pass: cut more than ten percent from the first complete rewrite; shorter paragraphs now do different jobs instead of repeating one lesson in equal-sized units.

Source pass: checked translation wording and editions, replaced mistaken anchors and PDF page destinations, marked literary/historical and textual/interpretive boundaries, and included substantive objections to the Laws, Forms, and philosopher rule.
Sentence-case headings, few emphases, contractions, and direct concrete claims; no em/en dashes or emojis.
uncertainties: No surviving accusers' speeches establish their motives or prove a concealed political prosecution.
Plato's speeches and prison scene cannot be independently verified as transcripts of the historical Socrates.
Early/middle/late groupings do not establish a clean boundary between Socrates' doctrines and Plato's.
The death threat in the cave may allude to Socrates, but the text does not identify the prisoner with him.
The Asclepius offering has competing interpretations; neither the English translations nor the dialogue settle its precise meaning.
The account of philosopher rule and the objections to it are editorial interpretations tied to identified passages, not claims about Ethan's lived experiences or personal beliefs.
This pass preserves existing inline layout. Root will apply and visually integrate the shared religious-text-inspired presentation.

first_editorial_passes.verdict_before: The 6,599-word working copy had a useful seven-stop structure and primary passages, but repeated the same moral in the introduction, section commentary, takeaway boxes, and conclusion. important_fixes: Replaced the promotion-and-money opening with the Ethics own qualification that loss of a child or friend can damage happiness. Kept external resources and luck inside the account of the good life.
Corrected the claim that happiness is the only good desired for itself. Book 1.7 also treats pleasure, honor, reason, and virtue as goods chosen for themselves, as well as for happiness.

Removed the argument that pleasure fails simply because it fades. Acknowledged the pleasures internal to excellent activity and Aristotle's own contemptuous treatment of a life devoted to bodily enjoyment.
Corrected the claim that happiness is only a verdict after death. Book 1.10 explicitly permits describing living people as happy, with qualifications about future changes.

Gave a real objection to the function argument: distinctiveness does not itself prove highest value. Removed the invented knife example as Aristotle's evidence and the unsupported claim that Irwin coined the function argument.
Replaced automatic habit formation with Book 2.4's conditions: knowledge, choice for the act's own sake, and settled character. Explained that practice can produce bad character too.

Corrected the implication that genuinely brave people are not miserable or pained. Book 3.9 specifically says wounds and death are painful and that good people can feel the loss of a good life especially strongly.

Corrected self-control to temperance in the mean table, named the deficiency in bodily pleasure, narrowed truthfulness to claims about oneself, and explained courage's two emotional dimensions. Kept the prohibition on a mean of theft, adultery, or murder.

Added the diet example for particular knowledge, equity in Book 5.10, and a short acknowledgment of akrasia in Book 7. Removed arbitrary ages, invented prodigies of sixteen, and the generalized claim that grey hair earns authority.

Removed unsupported claims that most friendships in our twenties fail by our thirties, that two or three lifetime friends is Aristotle's ideal, and that character friendship is unconditionally permanent. Added Book 9.3 on changed friends and noted that fullest friendship also includes pleasure and usefulness.

Kept contemplation's stronger ranking and divine comparison. Removed the smoothing conclusion that Aristotle merely advises room for the best hours. Kept the dispute over how Book 10 fits the earlier account, with a named scholarly interpretation.

Replaced the cynical rot-under-marble aside and claim that the machine simply runs better after removing prejudice. Named limitations inside both Politics and Ethics, and acknowledged that equal standing requires revising parts of Aristotle's account.

Corrected Ross's first-edition date from 1908 to 1925 using the edition's own front matter. Standardized all quoted excerpts to their source wording and preserved fragment boundaries rather than silently repairing punctuation.

Reduced the six-translation apparatus to one verified Bartlett-and-Collins comparison, with book, Bekker location, edition, and page. Removed unnecessary transliteration and translator generalizations.

Kept all seven station IDs and fixed a pre-existing scroll-spy mismatch that left the navigation label on the previous stop after using the index. Index opening now accurately updates aria-expanded and Escape restores focus.

length_decision.decision: Cut substantially while retaining all 28 selections. The reader now has complete explanation coverage; longer original-text translations remain available for context instead of reducing the whole work to isolated slogans.
length_decision.method: Word tokens counted after removing HTML markup. Static main excludes noscript and site navigation/footer. Loaded commentary includes all note titles, gist/read fields, Greek glosses and explanations before, and titles/plain explanations after. Translation totals count only English quotation text, including repeated versions; these are reported separately from editorial prose.
length_decision.introduction_read_time: The introduction is labeled 3 minutes, using 200 words per minute and rounding up.
length_decision.draft_self_edit: The separate final edit shortened the 28-explanation first draft by more than ten percent, after earlier removal of the old layered commentary and repeated interpretive codas.

voice_changes: Kept the concrete opening about being made into a Caesar after testing whether deleting the first paragraph lost information.
Applied the monotone, generic-sentence, volume-cut, and source passes, then a separate line-level self-edit.
Replaced motivational/productivity analogies with the passage's social purpose and its own language; varied explanation length and removed repeated defensive endings.
Reduced reflexive formatting, preserved useful short lexical notes, and removed blanket Greek-versus-English claims that the translations did not support.
No em/en dashes or emojis in any of the four changed files; title, og:title, and h1 match.
uncertainties: The received Greek and its online transcriptions have edition variants and occasional transcription defects. This review compares content and sources; it does not establish a new critical text or collate manuscripts.
Marcus's exact composition dates, ordering, intended eventual audience, and fidelity in governing to his own principles cannot be established from the passages.

The Hays excerpt was checked in an official publisher reproduction and an independent printed attribution, rather than a directly accessible page of the original 2002 hardcover. No other modern quote remains without equivalent support.
Casaubon's divisions do not align one-to-one with modern sections. His locators name the actual divisions used and excerpts may cross a division.
The minimal DOM checks verify script contracts and rendering content, not visual layout. Root still owns full browser validation and shared religious-text shell integration.

first_editorial_passes.verdict_before: The five-question comparison and navigation were worth keeping. The prose was substantially too repetitive, and its brisk summaries repeatedly crossed into caricature. The source labels promised verbatim wording while Hobbes and several other passages had been silently altered or excerpted without adequate disclosure.
important_fixes: Replaced all island/plane-crash framing, opening quote fan and five repeated split panels with concrete book arguments.
Corrected Hobbes on assembly sovereignty, retained self-defense, protection-dependent allegiance, and conquest-related consent; retained the weakness of checks on sovereign power.

Corrected Locke's two surrendered powers and broad use of property; added majority/tacit consent, law and tax limits, resistance threshold, spoilage/enough-and-as-good limits, and money-based inequality.

Separated Rousseau's conjectural history from Social Contract; distinguished sovereignty from executive government, general will from majority preference, changed forms of liberty, unanimous founding consent and excluded dissenters.
Kept racial/colonial and male-citizenship exclusions visible, while marking contested Locke authorship and contested colonial-dispossession inference. Added Rousseau's civil-religion coercion.
Removed simple direct claims connecting Locke to the Declaration, Rousseau to the French Revolution and forced to be free to modern totalitarianism.

Verified all 15 excerpts in their exact cited chapters and made each citation a source link. Distinguished 1689 publication from 1690 title-page date, and Cole's 1913 translation from the digitized 1920 volume.

first_editorial_passes.verdict_before: The seven-stop structure and primary excerpts were useful, but the 5,095-word page repeatedly treated Kant as a modern advice manual and overstated the certainty of his arguments. It conflated unconditional moral worth with all value, emotional indifference with duty, universalization with a mechanical logic test, consent with sufficient respect, and autonomy with freedom from appetite. Its strongest factual mistake called freedom itself the later fact of reason; it also claimed a direct identity between Kantian dignity and the UDHR and conflated lying examples.
important_fixes: Rebuilt all seven explanations around the actual Groundwork argument, retaining IDs, navigation, quoted passages, portrait assets and dedicated-script contract.
Distinguished good will from favorable outcomes and mere wishing; explained conforming to duty versus acting from duty without dismissing sympathy.
Added an explicitly reconstructed maxim, contradiction in conception versus will, perfect versus imperfect duties, and the four original examples with their contested premise.
Explained humanity as rational end-setting, merely-as-means, deception, positive duties and the limits of consent; corrected Preis/value and removed unsupported human-rights genealogy.
Replaced appetite, addiction and soldier metaphors with autonomy, heteronomy and the difficult freedom argument. Corrected the fact-of-reason claim and marked interpretive uncertainty.
Separated the 1797 lying essay from the lying promise, gave its legal and constrained setting, and stated the strongest objection with its assumptions.
Corrected Paton publisher to Hutchinson 1948, marked an omitted autonomy parenthesis, corrected the jewel locator, verified translator wording, and supplied direct primary and scholarly links.

Replaced blanket social-Darwinism exoneration with Darwin's actual 1871 tension between hereditary fears and sympathy. Kept distinction between biological account and moral instruction.

first_editorial_passes.verdict_before: The longest post in the set devoted roughly 7,000 words to an account that repeated the First Essay's slave-revolt mechanism while scarcely explaining the Genealogy's Second and Third Essays. It treated Nietzsche as the exceptional dissenter from a supposed agreement among all the other traditions, staged imagined conversations with the reader, softened will to power into personal improvement, and relied on a dramatic account of his sister to separate Nietzsche from nearly all disturbing political material. Several quotations were inaccurately credited or incompletely reproduced despite the blanket verbatim claim.
important_fixes: Rebuilt the introduction around the specific Tertullian passage Nietzsche discusses in Genealogy I.15. Removed invented reader conversations, the atheist lunch scene, repeated series-wide claims about humility, aphoristic endings, and recurring takeaways.

Distinguished Beyond Good and Evil (1886) from On the Genealogy of Morals (1887), and identified the earlier Gay Science and Zarathustra as the sources of the death of God, recurrence, and overman passages.

Explained master and slave valuation as patterns that can coexist in a society and a person, with self-command and generosity as well as contempt in master valuation. Removed the simple strong-person versus weak-person partition.

Explained ressentiment as persistent resentment that reorganizes judgment, distinguished Nietzsche's lambs-and-predators argument from a justification of human predation, and retained the objection that origin alone does not establish a rule's present value.

Replaced the repetitive fourth stop with the Second Essay's debt, guilt, internalized aggression, and punishment distinctions, followed by the Third Essay's different uses of asceticism, priestly interpretation of suffering, and unconditional commitment to truth.
Labeled the creditor history, Jewish-priestly origins, and internalization accounts as Nietzsche's conjectures or polemical reconstructions rather than established anthropology.

Explained will to power as including command over drives, artistic form, interpretation, domination, and exploitation. Marked Beyond Good and Evil 36 as conditional and distinguished the published text from notebook experiments.

Kept the overman passage and a compact Common/Kaufmann comparison without presenting the figure as a straightforward Aryan race or a universal self-improvement prescription. Added the authority problem in value legislation.

Distinguished eternal recurrence's hypothetical challenge in Gay Science 341 from a demonstrated scientific cosmology. Retained the objection that refusing to affirm trauma or atrocity need not mean failing to value life.

Kept Nietzsche's documented opposition to antisemitic movements and nationalism while retaining the racial stereotypes, hostile generalizations about Jews, rejection of women's equality, aristocratic sacrifice, and Antichrist 2. Removed the claim that a sister alone invented all objectionable content or that Nietzsche simply caused Nazism.
Reduced the illness account to the January 1889 collapse in Turin and death in 1900. Removed the horse story, diagnosis, unsupported mental-state claims, and theatrical death narrative.

Corrected the Genealogy I.10 excerpt's translator credit to Walter Kaufmann and R. J. Hollingdale. Corrected excerpt scope and cut marks; removed the faulty 'from henceforth' rendering of Gay Science 276 and the inaccurate opening wording of the earlier Gay Science 341 excerpt.

Made title, og:title, and h1 identical as 'Nietzsche and the Case Against Morality'; aligned both descriptions, added the summary/source IDs required by the presentation reference, and preserved all eight station IDs, labels/tags, image assets, and script references.

length_decision.counting_method: HTML comments and tags removed, entities decoded, then words counted with the Unicode pattern \b[\w]+(?:[’'-][\w]+)*\b. Counts cover the visible hero and main, including captions, passage labels and quotations, walking labels, the collapsed comparison, and source prose. They exclude head metadata, CSS, scripts, footer, and endcap navigation. Main-only counts are supplied separately.
length_decision.read_time: 13 min read, rounded up from 2,745 visible hero/main words at 220 words per minute.
length_decision.rationale: This substantial cut removes repeated explanatory scaffolding and sensational biography while expanding coverage to all three Genealogy essays. The remaining length earns its place through the valuation mechanism, guilt/asceticism, positive ideals, and concrete objections. No arbitrary word target was used.
largest_cuts: The invented atheist lunchtime dialogue and blanket claims that every other tradition teaches the same surrender.
Repeated slave-revolt explanations, virtue interrogation, and concluding takeaway panels.
A long parade of modern analogies and self-improvement prompts attached to will to power and the overman.
The extended sister/theft drama, funeral and Hitler anecdotes, Paraguay story, horse story, and diagnosis.
Long passages where a shorter existing excerpt preserves the argument; claims that every excerpt was verbatim despite unmarked changes.

five_passes: Generic-sentence pass: replaced the inflated series introduction with Tertullian's specific condemned-persecutors episode and attached the work and section immediately.
Cadence pass: removed recurring punchlines, dialogue, staged revelations, and identical lesson-summary structures; varied paragraph lengths according to the mechanism being explained.
Credibility pass: identified speculative genealogies, conditional power theory, competing recurrence readings, manuscript limits, and textual exclusions without sanitizing or overclaiming.
Warmth pass: treated the reader as an interested reader of the texts, with no invented beliefs, lunchtime experiences, scolding, or demands for personal confession.

Mechanical pass: checked title equality, descriptions, section locators, translator credits, cut marks, long dashes and encoded dashes, emoji ranges, hard and soft voice-lint phrases, station IDs, and internal targets.
voice_changes.separate_self_edit: Saved a complete first rewrite as nietzsche-draft.html, then independently reread and revised the finished page. This cut another 307 visible words, 10.06%, tightened the speculative-history explanations, removed rhetorical signposts and repeated distinctions, and corrected the fable objection and source-link precision.

uncertainties: The replacement of Christian values by a coherent positive account is philosophically contested. The article identifies the authority, suffering, and affirmation problems instead of pretending they are settled.
Will to power and recurrence have contested interpretive roles. Their conjectural or conditional formulations are distinguished from established scientific claims.
The Christmas 1887 letter is cited to Kaufmann's edition and its date label. The surviving manuscript and sending history were not independently authenticated.

The Mission17 Genealogy excerpt is an image-only scan. Retained English wording was checked against an indexed University of Illinois excerpt; translator credit was independently checked against a library record. The linked Mission17 image itself was not fully OCR-verified.
Direct NietzscheSource German section URLs did not load. Editorial-method claims are supported by the accessible project documentation; no German critical passage is falsely claimed as inspected.
Illness diagnosis and memorable biographical anecdotes were removed rather than retained with uncertain evidence.
No browser or visual QA was performed by this editor. Root owns the shared presentation and browser verification. The dedicated JavaScript was deliberately unchanged.

Gives Nagel’s internal-conflict diagnosis, larger-purpose objection, and irony substantial treatment; keeps the objection about the logical need for revolt and the ethical limits of conscious experience.

first_editorial_passes.verdict_before: The old page had worthwhile original passages and working diagrams, but repeated exposition, paraphrase, applause, and takeaway layers made it much too long. It overstated the wager as costless, attributed infinite hell to the matrix, conflated two outcomes with equal probability, misidentified Lewis as an Oxford professor during the broadcasts, and treated the trilemma as a settled victory. Its claim that these arguments never converted a committed atheist was unsupported.
important_fixes: Rebuilt the article around the difference between practical reasons to seek faith and evidential reasons to believe Christianity.
Corrected Pensées publication to the posthumous 1670 edition, kept composition date uncertain, and identified Brunschvicg 233, Lafuma 418, Sellier 680 and the W.F. Trotter translation.
Reconstructed the wager with infinite salvation and finite other outcomes. The matrix explicitly omits rival religions and does not assert that Pascal’s argument requires infinite punishment.

Explained why the final expected-utility argument requires positive probability rather than 50/50 odds; retained substantial finite costs, voluntary-belief difficulties, Pascal’s recommended practices, and the ambiguity of vous abêtira.

Gave the many-gods objection and the defender’s evidence-based reply, the mixed-strategy infinity tie, undefined calculations with positive and negative infinities, and the need for alternative comparison rules.
Corrected Lewis’s Oxford fellowship/tutorial role, his 1954 Cambridge professorship, the four 1941 to 44 BBC series, and the August 6, 1941 first broadcast after the main Blitz.
Distinguished naturalistic explanations of moral judgment from the truth and authority of moral obligations; neither evolutionary origins nor intense moral feelings alone settle the question.

Presented the trilemma as conditional on the historical attribution and interpretation of Jesus’s claims. Removed claims of historical certainty, caricatures of believers and skeptics, and the unsupported universal assertion about atheist conversion.

Retained four gallery cards only because each examines a distinct premise: knowing deception, sincere error, a true claim, and the records. Removed all repeated verdict paragraphs and made their rendering optional.
Retained two brief primary blockquotes with explicit locators and one four-word Lewis quotation. Replaced the other long extracted passages with shorter, labeled paraphrase and analysis.
Reduced the source list to eight substantive entries, updated both descriptions and the ten-minute estimate, and preserved the main section IDs and gallery contracts.

findings.location: aristotle.html:340, #st-phronesis, paragraph beginning 'Knowing better still doesn't ensure doing better.'
findings.problem: Immediately after the account of phronesis, this paragraph can make weakness of will sound like a failure of fully acquired practical wisdom. Aristotle explicitly denies that the practically wise person can be akratic in Ethics 7.10, 1152a6-15. His explanation distinguishes possessing knowledge from actively using it, and practical wisdom from mere cleverness. The current sentences about ordinary better judgment are reasonable, but the transition leaves that important distinction implicit.
findings.proposed_fix: Make the ordinary-knowledge point directly and keep the paragraph short, for example: 'A person can know what they should do and fail to act on it. Book 7 investigates akrasia, weakness of will: appetite or anger can prevent that knowledge from guiding action. Aristotle distinguishes this from practical wisdom, which requires good character and the ability to act.' Link Book 7 as now; do not expand into a new discussion.

findings.problem: Three explanatory passages finish by restating a limitation that nearby concrete analysis already establishes. The forgiveness sentence at 243 repeats the stronger origin-versus-current-value paragraph at 245. The final notebook/doctrine sentence at 277 repeats both the immediately preceding hypothesis sentence and the textual distinction developed at 328. The last sentence at 312 announces that the thought experiment does not prove a failure to live well, after the paragraph has already supplied the concrete trauma objection. Together they contribute to the repeated corrective-coda cadence root asked us to inspect.
findings.proposed_fix: Delete the second sentence at 243 ('That charge does not show...'); keep the concrete section-14 attribution. At 277 delete the final notebook/doctrine sentence while keeping the disputed scope, conditional section 36 and biology/physics distinction. At 312 delete the last sentence, leaving the concrete objection and the sentence 'Nietzsche's demand for affirmation is exceptionally high.' Preserve the substantive objections at 242, 245 and 262, which do real explanatory work.

findings.problem: The cognitive-revolution paragraph already says mutation is a possible explanation and that Harari acknowledges the unknown cause, then adds two more sentences saying it is a hypothesis and unproved. The future paragraph labels the successor scenario speculative, then pre-emptively rejects a gene-therapy inference that the next paragraph handles concretely. findings.proposed_fix: At 211 remove 'That remains a hypothesis. The book does not demonstrate such a mutation.' Keep the actual date range, the attribution of a possible genetic explanation, the unknown cause and the sentence about artifacts not dating the first stories. At 337 remove the last sentence ('A gene therapy doesn't tell us whether human beings will be replaced.'); keep the speculation label and the FDA paragraph's explicit distinction between edited blood-forming stem cells and a heritable lineage. Keep the regional/sample limits at 311-315 and the association-versus-causation distinction at 328, which are substantive.
